comments.author: @fubarbaz
comments.text: It is maddening to hear otherwise intelligent people fumble in their reasoning about what society can and can’t do by making appeals to money constraints. The government has infinite money, and a monopoly on its creation. The actual resources and productive capacity of society are what determines what can actually be distributed. Everyone agrees that super intelligence can in principle effectuate drastic increases in productive capacity and efficiency of resource utilization, which will lead to commensurate increases in societal wealth. What remains to decide is the balance between consumption and investment (do you want to delay some consumption so as to increase total consumption over time), and the character and mechanism of distribution. To be clear, I believe the distribution problem is insoluble, and we’re all going to end up serfs if we’re lucky, but that is where the conversation should be focused. It’s not ‘can we afford a UBI’, it’s ’is UBI the mechanism of distribution we want to employ, and whatever mechanism we choose, do we have the political power to force its implementation, and if we don’t, how do we get the necessary political power?’

So, I took the transcript, fed it into my AI that I gave a specialized system prompt that evaluates factual information and noise from statistically accurate data, and this is what I got:

1. He’s right on direction, aggressive on timeline & absolutes.
2. Reasonable framing; overstated as “the economic engine is only GPUs.”
3. He’s using “UBI doesn’t work” as a foil to pitch his dual-currency design.
4. This is startup whitepaper territory: interesting, not inevitable.
5. This is poetic; don’t build policy on it.
6. He’s directionally right on the hollowing out of generic knowledge work, but wrong to generalize that to "you have no value."
7. His curve is steep; reality likely more stepwise and sector-specific but still rough.
8. He's not crazy to worry.
9. He’s right that “just tax Big Tech for UBI” math is simplistic.
10. On Universal personal AI Agents: This is one of the most credible and important parts. If you’re thinking strategically for yourself or for policy, assume this.

comments.author: @ceneezer
comments.text:
Here's an interesting thought:   I've absorbed some 110M tokens this year through youtube alone. (and many multiples of that through chats)
I've likely churned that into about 1M tokens output, using tools, but not including gfx.

Short answer up front: if we count just the spoken/reading language in 20 hours of YouTube per day, a human would process on the order of ~200,000–480,000 language tokens per day (depending on speaking/reading speed). Below are the clean assumptions and the math.

Assumptions

20 hours = 20 × 60 = 1,200 minutes = 72,000 seconds.

1 token ≈ 0.75 words (common rough OpenAI convention), so tokens = words ÷ 0.75 = words × 1.3333….

Typical speaking speeds:

Slow/clear talk: 120 words/minute (wpm)

Conversational: 150 wpm (baseline)

Fast speech: 180 wpm

Fast reading/scanning captions: ~300 wpm

Calculations (digit-by-digit shown)

Words in 20 hr = minutes × wpm = 1,200 × wpm.

Tokens = words × 1.333333...

For each wpm:

120 wpm

words = 1,200 × 120 = 144,000 words

tokens = 144,000 × 1.3333333 = 192,000 tokens

tokens per second = 192,000 ÷ 72,000 = 2.67 tokens/sec

150 wpm (typical)

words = 1,200 × 150 = 180,000 words

tokens = 180,000 × 1.3333333 = 240,000 tokens

tokens per second = 240,000 ÷ 72,000 = 3.33 tokens/sec

180 wpm

words = 1,200 × 180 = 216,000 words

tokens = 216,000 × 1.3333333 = 288,000 tokens

tokens per second = 288,000 ÷ 72,000 = 4.00 tokens/sec

300 wpm (fast caption-reading)

words = 1,200 × 300 = 360,000 words

tokens = 360,000 × 1.3333333 = 480,000 tokens

tokens per second = 480,000 ÷ 72,000 = 6.67 tokens/sec

Quick per-hour and per-minute figures (baseline 150 wpm)

Per hour (150 wpm): 12,000 tokens/hour.

Per minute (150 wpm): 200 tokens/minute.

Context & caveats

These numbers are language-token equivalents (spoken audio or captions). They match how language-model tokens map roughly to words — useful for comparing to model context windows (for scale: 240k tokens ≫ typical 32k token context windows).

Visual information (images, motion, faces, graphs) is not captured by "tokens" in the language sense. Converting visual stream to tokens would require defining an encoding (e.g., image tokens or bits/frame) and gives numbers orders of magnitude larger — so I avoided that because it’s highly model-dependent and speculative.

Real YouTube content varies (silence, music, dense lecture text, pauses). So treat the ranges above as order-of-magnitude estimates.

The National Wealth Prosperity Model: Britain’s Path to a Self-Reliant and Abundant Future
In a world where economic systems often feel like they’re designed to serve a select few, the National Wealth Prosperity Model (NWPM) offers a refreshing alternative—one rooted in British ingenuity and focused on putting our nation’s strength back in the hands of its people. Imagine an economy where energy isn’t just a bill to pay, but the very foundation of our currency, where households become mini power stations contributing to the national grid, and where we break free from the cycles of debt and dependency that have held us back. This model isn’t about patching up the old ways; it’s a complete reimagining, inspired by the idea of a post-scarcity society like the one in Star Trek, where replicators and infinite energy make abundance the norm. Here in Britain, we have adequate resources that, when optimized, can feel infinite too. The NWPM turns that vision into reality, projecting substantial wealth growth, steady economic expansion, and stronger communities—all while fostering self-reliance and social cohesion. Let’s explore what makes this model tick, why it’s needed, and how it could change our future for the better.
The Inspiration: Thinking Backwards for a Forward Leap When I first conceived the NWPM, I flipped the usual economic thinking on its head. Instead of starting with scarcity—limited resources, endless competition, and profit at any cost—I asked: What if we had replicators and infinite energy, like on the Starship Enterprise? How would our economy work then? In that world, people contribute for fulfillment, not survival, and technology handles the basics. Britain isn’t there yet, but we have enough—adequate energy, resources, and talent—that we can treat them as functionally infinite through smart management. This shifts our culture from consuming energy to create assets and manage money, to creating and conserving energy to build true wealth. It’s a mindset change: productivity without the daily grind, where AI and robotics free us for meaningful roles, making the NWPM a smarter alternative to universal basic income by rewarding contribution over passivity.
Why We Need Change: The Flaws in Our Current Setup and What’s Coming Our current economy is like an old engine running on fumes—complicated taxes that hit hardworking families hard, energy bills that swing with global whims, and a financial system that often feels like it’s slicing up our national wealth for a quick profit, shipping billions overseas while we cover the losses. Communities are feeling the strain, with jobs disappearing to automation and regions left behind. Inflation quietly eats away at savings, acting like a hidden tax that benefits those who engineer the system by reducing debt’s real value, but leaves everyone else poorer.
Looking ahead, the challenges grow. AI and robots could displace millions of jobs, energy demands are set to rise sharply with tech’s expansion, and global pressures—like corporate-driven digital IDs and a “stakeholder” economy—threaten our independence, potentially turning us into dependents on multinational agendas. Without a shift, we’ll face deeper divides, more debt, and less control over our own destiny.
The Guiding Principles: Self-Reliance, Cohesion, and Abundance The NWPM is built on ideas that put Britain first, creating a system where we stand strong together. We keep the pound as our everyday currency—something tangible and trusted—while going digital for transactions, with government in charge of IDs to keep corporations at bay. Energy is central: our money ties to what we produce at home, so prices for goods naturally adjust with energy use, guiding us toward smarter, greener choices without heavy rules.
We empower the government to cut ties with those asset managers who’ve loaded us with debt, then wipe it clean—a fresh start that frees us to invest in ourselves. Taxes simplify to a light touch on deals, hitting global finance harder to make them contribute fairly. Energy isn’t traded for profit; it’s shared, with homes and communities pitching in surplus to earn rewards that bind us closer. Small businesses get room to breathe, thriving in a market for most goods while we protect what’s vital. It’s not about chasing gains at any cost—it’s about abundance through teamwork, where productivity comes from contribution, not just clocking in, turning AI’s threats into opportunities for a richer life.
How the Model Works: Mechanics and Real-World Application The NWPM centers on energy as the key to everything. We ramp up production to 355 TWh, with homes and communities adding 5–15 TWh of surplus, managed by the Energy Prosperity Authority to keep things steady. Simple kits let millions generate power, sell what’s extra, and pocket rewards—turning everyday folks into partners in our national grid. Community projects like shared solar or wind setups expand this, with storage batteries smoothing out peaks and dips for reliability.
Our digital pound, pegged to this energy base, keeps inflation low and stable. The Nationalist Central Bank lends to British businesses, keeping profits home, while pensions build a massive Wealth Reserve for everyone. Taxes become a straightforward levy on transactions, funding infrastructure, tech, and more—delivering growth and jobs without the old burdens. We start with pilots in 2025—testing digital setups, energy kits, and debt relief—scaling up by 2027, with the full vision in place by the decade’s end. It’s practical, with built-in flexibility for our non-infinite world.
The Upsides: Why This Beats What We Have Now Compared to today’s setup, the NWPM shines in stability and strength. Our current pound swings with markets, but this energy tie keeps things steady, avoiding those costly shocks. We save big on imports, keep wealth local, and cut admin hassles with smart tech. Growth doubles what we’re expecting, jobs multiply in meaningful ways, and communities get direct boosts—more money circulating where it matters. It’s a system that values contribution, turning potential job losses from tech into chances for innovation and balance.
The Downsides and How We Fix Them Every big idea has hurdles, but the NWPM’s are fixable and often no worse than what we face now. Spending might dip a bit from the new levy, but phasing it in and offering reliefs offset that. Evasion risks are low with blockchain, and energy price wobbles get smoothed by buffers and community storage. Debt focus on home investments has risks, but AI tools and diversification keep them in check. Dynamic prices could fluctuate, but central oversight makes it manageable. Overall, these are handled with smart tweaks like grants for kits and public input, making the model even stronger.
A Honest Wrap-Up: The Road Ahead In wrapping up, the NWPM is Britain’s blueprint for a brighter tomorrow—delivering wealth growth, steady expansion, and tighter communities through energy-driven abundance. It outshines our current system in stability, self-sufficiency, and fairness, with challenges that we can tackle head-on. With careful steps, it could transform us; without, some bumps along the way. But this is our chance for a sovereign, united Britain—let’s seize it.

The argument against UBI is a weak strawman. I agree that funding UBI up to poverty level income would be difficult. The notion that less than this would be inadequate is a false dichotomy because UBI (unlike needs based welfare) does not preclude other income. Think of it this way: we currently have UBI at $0/mo. The question is whether $0/mo is the economically optimal amount. At low levels, UBI will greatly increase velocity of money, increase demand and significantly offset the decrease in profits associated with increased taxes. Funding with corporate tax would be optimal insofar as UBI can increase with degree of automation, ensuring a market for products produced at costs that asymptotically approach zero. Income tax at the highest brackets would be good too, since doing so would have no impact on incentive to invest well (because the relative proportional payoff would be unchanged).
